scholar: Pliny the Younger (letter to Trajan; the Christians' own account as reported by Pliny)
work: Epistulae X.96 (letter to Trajan), c. 111-113 AD
edition: Platner, Samuel Ball, Selections from the Letters of the Younger Pliny, Boston: Leach, Shewell and Sanborn, 1894 (Latin text stated to follow Keil, ed. minor). Archive.org item selectionsfromle00pilirich.
quote_orig: Adfirmabant autem hanc fuisse summam vel culpae suae vel erroris, quod essent soliti stato die ante lucem convenire carmenque Christo quasi deo dicere secum invicem, seque Sacramento non in scelus aliquod obstringere, sed ne furta, ne latrocinia, ne adulteria committerent, ne fidem fallerent, ne depositum appellati abnegarent.
context_before: Pliny reports what people who were denounced as Christians told him under questioning: they had only met before dawn on a fixed day. The quoted sentence is their own description of what they did.
what_it_says: They said their fault or error was to meet before dawn on a fixed day and to sing a carmen to Christ "as to a god" (quasi deo), then bind themselves by oath to avoid theft, robbery, adultery and breach of trust.
claim_supported: (C) early worship of Jesus; (D) background only in the sense that it is a non-Christian witness
scholar_qualification: This is a Roman governor reporting, under torture and interrogation, what the accused said; "quasi deo" is Pliny's wording of what they sang. The Dickinson College commentary (Francese, Pliny Selected Letters, 10.96) glosses carmen as "hymn," or "perhaps better 'responsive reading' or liturgy; dicere rather favors the latter (Kingery)". So "sang a hymn" is one reading, not the only one. It says nothing about Jesus' own claims.
source_url: https://archive.org/download/selectionsfromle00pilirich/selectionsfromle00pilirich.pdf (PDF); OCR text https://archive.org/download/selectionsfromle00pilirich/selectionsfromle00pilirich_djvu.txt; second Latin witness with macrons: https://dcc.dickinson.edu/pliny-letters/10-96
limits: Latin read in the archive.org OCR and in the PDF page image (PDF p. 101 = printed p. 91; PNG at dl/page_platner_pdf101.png). Platner's text lacks macrons; the Dickinson page has the same sentence with macrons (verified). English translation: Fordham Medieval Sourcebook page (translator not named; https://sourcebooks.web.fordham.edu/source/pliny1.asp) read but not attributed, so not used as a verbatim source. Not checked: the Melmoth 1746 translation (not obtained).

scholar: Ignatius of Antioch (Epistle to the Romans, opening greeting)
work: Epistle to the Romans, c. 110 AD (Ignatian letters)
edition: Roberts, Alexander and James Donaldson, trans., Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885, public domain), as reproduced on ellopos.net (Shorter and Longer Versions heading)
page: page unknown (ANF vol. 1 page not seen)
quote_orig: the Church which is beloved and enlightened by the will of Him that willeth all things which are according to the love of Jesus Christ our God, which also presides in the place of the region of the Romans
context_before: The greeting praises the Roman church, addressed as a church blessed through the majesty of the Most High Father and "Jesus Christ, His only-begotten Son".
what_it_says: The Roman church is described as blessed by the will of God "which are according to the love of Jesus Christ our God".
claim_supported: (B) earliest Christians call Jesus "our God" in a greeting formula (c. 110 AD); (C) early devotion, weakly
scholar_qualification: The phrase depends on the recension and translation. The Lightfoot 1889 rendering of the same greeting (archive.org item bwb_S0-DRH-400_3, OCR) reads "to her who presideth in the place of the country of the Romans" with no "our God", so the wording is not secure. A greeting formula is weaker evidence than a sustained title.
limits: Read as an English translation on a web page, not a page image; the Greek was not read. Recension variation and translation variation are unresolved. Lightfoot (1889 OCR) variant noted above.

scholar: Ignatius of Antioch (Epistle to the Ephesians, opening greeting)
work: Epistle to the Ephesians, c. 110 AD (Ignatian letters)
edition: Roberts and Donaldson, ANF vol. 1 (1885), as reproduced on ellopos.net, page 7 of the Ephesians pages
page: page unknown (ANF vol. 1 page not seen)
quote_orig: being united and elected through the true passion by the will of the Father, and Jesus Christ, our God: Abundant happiness through Jesus Christ, and His undefiled grace.
context_before: The Ephesians greeting, in the form printed first on the page. The same page prints the longer-version greeting right after it.
what_it_says: In the shorter-version greeting the church is "elected ... by the will of the Father, and Jesus Christ, our God".
claim_supported: (B) earliest Christians call Jesus "our God" in an early letter
scholar_qualification: The longer-version greeting on the same page reads "by the will of God the Father, and of our Lord Jesus Christ our Saviour" (not "our God"). The Lightfoot 1889 OCR of the Ephesians greeting reads "by the will of the Father of Jesus Christ our God" (no "Jesus Christ, our God" construction). So the phrase is in some versions but is not stable across the recensions. It also does not show Jesus speaking as YHWH.
limits: Web translation, not a page image; the Greek was not read. The Lightfoot OCR inscription (archive.org bwb_S0-DRH-400_3) was read in the OCR text, without a page number.

edition: King James Version (public domain)
quote_orig: If any man love not the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be Anathema Maranatha.
context_before: Paul closes 1 Corinthians with a curse on anyone who does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, using the Aramaic word.
what_it_says: Paul uses the Aramaic "Maranatha" in a curse formula alongside "the Lord Jesus Christ".
claim_supported: (C) early worship of Jesus (the Aramaic invocation is the usual evidence); (E) the reading "Our Lord, come" versus "The Lord has come" is debated
scholar_qualification: The sentence alone does not say Maranatha is addressed to Jesus; the usual argument (Hurtado, Bauckham) depends on reading the phrase as a prayer to the Lord. That reading is contested and was not checked against the scholarship.
limits: KJV wording read verbatim. KJV (public domain) read via bible-api.com; the Greek was not checked against NA28 or another critical text. The Greek "Μαρανα θα" was not checked; the Cambridge essay on Maranatha surfaced in search but was not read.

scholar: Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles), chapter 10
work: Didache, late 1st or early 2nd century (date disputed)
edition: Lightfoot, J.B., The Apostolic Fathers (archive.org item apostolicfathers18812ligh, OCR text; running header "The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles. 175" appears just before the passage in the OCR)
page: p. 175 (per running header in OCR; not checked against the page image)
quote_orig: Let grace come and let this world pass away. Hosanna to the Son of David! Whoever is holy, let him come ; whoever is not, let him repent. Maranatha. Amen.
context_before: The end of the Eucharistic thanksgiving prayer in chapter 10 of the Didache, after the prayer for the Church gathered from the four winds into the kingdom.
what_it_says: The prayer closes with "Maranatha" after an invitation for the holy to come and the unholy to repent.
claim_supported: (C) early worship of Jesus in a liturgical setting (contested: the prayer may be addressed to God)
scholar_qualification: The later Lightfoot edition in the same archive OCR (apostolicfathers00ligh) renders the same passage as "May grace come ... Hosanna to the God of David ... Maran Atha. Amen.", so "Son of David" versus "God of David" is a translation or edition difference. Whether Maranatha is addressed to Jesus is debated and not settled here.
limits: Read in OCR of an English translation, not a page image; the Greek was not checked; the page number comes from a running header in the OCR text and is not confirmed on the scan. Both Lightfoot OCR texts read.

edition: Roberts, Alexander and James Donaldson, trans., ANF vol. 1 (1885), as reproduced by Logos Virtual Library
page: page unknown (ANF vol. 1 page not seen)
quote_orig: But both Him, and the Son (who came forth from Him and taught us these things, and the host of the other good angels who follow and are made like to Him), and the prophetic Spirit, we worship and adore, knowing them in reason and truth, and declaring without grudging to every one who wishes to learn, as we have been taught.
context_before: Justin answers the charge of atheism: Christians are atheists only with respect to the gods of myth, not "the most true God, the Father of righteousness and temperance".
what_it_says: Justin says Christians worship and adore the Father, the Son and the prophetic Spirit, and he distinguishes the Son as one who "came forth from Him".
claim_supported: (C) early worship of Jesus (the Son is worshipped in a list with the Father and the Spirit)
scholar_qualification: The sentence shows worship of the Son alongside the Father, but Justin also says the Son "came forth from" the Father and lists him with "the host of the other good angels". That is a subordinationist framework, which does not match a claim that Jesus is YHWH in the Gospel sense.
limits: English translation read verbatim on a web page; the Greek was not read; no page number of the printed ANF volume was seen.

scholar: Lucian of Samosata (The Passing of Peregrinus, sect. 11)
edition: Fowler, H.W. and F.G. Fowler, trans., The Works of Lucian of Samosata, vol. 4, Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1905 (public domain), as reproduced on Perseus/CTS (cts.perseids.org)
page: p. 82 (inferred: Perseus page marker "v.4.p.83" appears after this passage; not checked against the printed page)
quote_orig: The Christians, you know, worship a man to this day,—the distinguished personage who introduced their novel rites, and was crucified on that account.
context_before: Lucian has just said that the Christians "took him for a God, accepted his laws, and declared him their president" (Peregrinus). He then names the man they worship as the crucified founder of their rites.
what_it_says: An outside observer reports that Christians worshipped a man who was crucified for introducing their rites.
claim_supported: (C) early worship of Jesus, from a hostile outside witness
scholar_qualification: Lucian is a satirist writing about a charlatan; he is not a careful reporter of Christian doctrine, and the passage tells us what he thought Christians did, not what Jesus claimed. The crucified figure is identified only by the context. The sentence itself is clear.
limits: English read, not Greek; page 82 is inferred from a page-break marker, not seen on the printed book; Perseus gives "v.4.p.83" after the passage.

edition: King James Version (public domain)
quote_orig: Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: That at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things  in heaven, and things in earth, and things under the earth; And that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
context_before: The hymn-like passage in 2:5-8 describes Christ taking the form of a servant and being obedient to death; 2:9-11 is his exaltation.
what_it_says: God exalts Jesus and gives him a name above every name, so that every knee bows at it.
claim_supported: (C) early worship of Jesus; (B) with Isa 45:23 in background (see J11-12 Bauckham)
scholar_qualification: The passage itself does not say the name is YHWH; that identification comes from scholars such as Bauckham reading it against Isa 45:22-23 (see J11-12).

scholar: Codex Sinaiticus (manuscript, 4th c.), transcription on codexsinaiticus.org
edition: Codex Sinaiticus Project transcription (handler transcription.ashx, quire 90, folio 1, side v, type=1)
quote_orig: εγω ειμι το αλφα και εγω και το ω αρχη και τελοϲ λεγει κϲ ο θϲ ο ων και ο ην και ο ερχομενοϲ ο παντοκρατωρ
context_before: Rev 1:4-8 opens the book with greeting and then a divine speech, which begins "I am the Alpha and the Omega".
what_it_says: English gloss (mine, not a translation from a source): the transcribed Greek has the Alpha-and-Omega clause with "beginning and end" (archē kai telos) and "the Lord God" (kurios ho theos) as the speaker.
claim_supported: (E) textual evidence on the wording of Rev 1:8; the speaker (God or Christ) is not settled by the manuscript
scholar_qualification: The transcription itself does not say whether "Lord God" in 1:8 refers to the Father or to Christ; that is an interpretive question. The critical texts (WH 1881, Nestle 1904, UBS4 variants, Byzantine 2005) print "Κύριος ὁ θεός" (see J11-11).
limits: Read from the site handler transcription, not from the folio image; the site uses symbols (┬) and reading marks not explained here; I did not verify against the image or a facsimile. Whether "αρχη και τελοϲ" is the first hand or a correction was not checked.

edition: Codex Sinaiticus Project transcription (handler, quire 90, folio 1, side v)
quote_orig: λεγουϲηϲ ┬ γραψον ειϲ το βιβλιον ┬ πεμψον ταιϲ επτα εκκληϲιαιϲ
context_before: Rev 1:10-11: John hears a voice behind him like a trumpet saying "write in a book" and send to the seven churches.
what_it_says: In the Sinaiticus transcription 1:11 goes straight from "saying" to "write in a book"; the clause "I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last" is absent.
claim_supported: (E) textual evidence: Sinaiticus lacks the Rev 1:11 clause (as transcribed)
scholar_qualification: This is one manuscript reading. It does not decide the question for Rev 1:8, 1:17, 2:8, 21:6 or 22:13, which are in the same book and have the same "Alpha and Omega" phrasing in Sinaiticus (see J11-12).
limits: Transcription only (folio image not checked). The site marks "┬" appear inside the line; I did not verify that the clause is absent from the original rather than erased or omitted by the transcriber.

scholar: Multiple Greek editions as shown on Biblehub (Nestle 1904, WH 1881, Tischendorf 8th, Stephanus 1550, Scrivener TR 1894, Byzantine Majority 2005)
edition: Biblehub multi-text page (biblehub.com/multi/revelation/1-8.htm and 1-11.htm)
quote_orig: Nestle 1904, Rev 1:8: λέγει Κύριος ὁ Θεός, ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος, ὁ Παντοκράτωρ. | Stephanus TR 1550, Rev 1:8: Ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω ἀρχὴ καὶ τέλος, λέγει ὁ κύριος ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος ὁ παντοκράτωρ | Nestle 1904, Rev 1:11: λεγούσης Ὃ βλέπεις γράψον εἰς βιβλίον καὶ πέμψον ταῖς ἑπτὰ ἐκκλησίαις | Tischendorf 8th and Stephanus 1550, Rev 1:11: λεγούσης, Ἐγώ ἐιμι τὸ Α καὶ τὸ Ω, ὁ πρῶτος καὶ ὁ ἔσχατος
context_before: Biblehub prints many Greek editions side by side for each verse.
what_it_says: The Alpha-and-Omega clause at Rev 1:11 is omitted in Nestle 1904, WH 1881 and the Byzantine Majority 2005 (as shown) and present in Tischendorf 8th, Stephanus 1550 and Scrivener TR 1894. At Rev 1:8, "beginning and end" is in the TR texts and not in Nestle 1904 or WH; "Lord God" is in Nestle, WH and Byzantine 2005.
claim_supported: (E) textual evidence on Rev 1:8 and 1:11 across editions
scholar_qualification: Biblehub is a secondary display of editions, not the NA28 or UBS apparatus; the bracketing and the committee rating for Rev 1:11 in NA28 were not seen. The Tischendorf 8th text includes the clause at 1:11 even though Sinaiticus as transcribed does not, which needs checking.
limits: Edition labels and Greek were read in the page HTML; the Tischendorf and Byzantine blocks were matched by label order and may be mis-assigned; NA28 and Metzger (1994) not obtained; apparatus of NA28 not seen.

edition: Codex Sinaiticus Project transcription (handler, quire 90 f.1 v; quire 90 f.2 r; quire 91 f.1 r and v)
quote_orig: Rev 1:17: εγω ειμι ο πρωτοϲ και ο εϲχατοϲ | Rev 2:8: ταδε λεγει ο πρωτοϲ και ο εϲχατοϲ οϲ εγενετο νεκροϲ και εζηϲεν | Rev 21:6: και λεγει μοι γεγονα εγω το αλφα και το ω η αρχη και το τελοϲ | Rev 22:13: εγω το αλφα και το ω ο πρωτοϲ κ(αι) ο εϲχατοϲ η αρχη κ(αι) το τελοϲ
context_before: Rev 1:17 is the risen Christ speaking to John ("Fear not; I am the first and the last"); Rev 2:8 is Christ addressing Smyrna; Rev 21:6 is a speech from the one on the throne (21:5) and 22:13 is a first-person speech in the closing section (22:12 has Christ saying he is coming).
what_it_says: Sinaiticus (as transcribed) has "the first and the last" at 1:17 and 2:8 and "Alpha and Omega, the first and the last" at 22:13 and "the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end" at 21:6. So the phrase is present in Sinaiticus outside Rev 1:11.
claim_supported: (A) Jesus speaks in the first person with a title that Isa 44:6 and 48:12 give to YHWH (in the Sinaitic text of 1:17, 2:8 and 22:13); (E) manuscript evidence
scholar_qualification: The transcription records readings only. The identification of the speaker is an exegetical question. The title "the first and the last" is YHWH's in Isa 44:6 and 48:12 in the KJV (read; Hebrew and LXX not checked), but whether Revelation intends that identification is not settled by the text alone.
limits: Transcription only (folio images not checked); Rev 22:20 "ναι ερχομαι ταχυ" also read in the transcription (quire 91 f.2 r); the Greek was not compared against the Alexandrinus.

scholar: Gospel of John (the Jewish reaction to Jesus' claim)
edition: King James Version (public domain)
quote_orig: I and my Father are one. Then the Jews took up stones again to stone him. Jesus answered them, Many good works have I shewed you from my Father; for which of those works do ye stone me? The Jews answered him, saying, For a good work we stone thee not; but for blasphemy; and because that thou, being a man, makest thyself God.
context_before: Jesus has said "I and my Father are one"; the Jews take up stones again.
what_it_says: The Jews say they stone him for blasphemy because he, "being a man, makest thyself God."
claim_supported: (A) Jesus is portrayed as claiming identity with the Father (the hearers take it as making himself God); (E) the Gospel reports this as the charge
scholar_qualification: This is the Gospel narrator's report of the charge, not a confirmed historical event. Ehrman (J11-19) reads the Johannine claims as theology, not history.
limits: KJV (public domain) read via bible-api.com; the Greek was not checked against NA28 or another critical text.

scholar: Gospel of Mark (the blasphemy charge over forgiveness)
edition: King James Version (public domain)

context_before: Jesus says to a paralysed man "Son, thy sins be forgiven thee."

work: "Complexities Surrounding God's Oneness in Biblical Monotheism", pp. 7-18 in Monotheism and Its Complexities (2018); also Jesus and the God of Israel (2008), a revised form of God Crucified (1998)
edition: Mosher, Lucinda A. and David Marshall, eds. Monotheism and Its Complexities: Christian and Muslim Perspectives. Washington, DC: Georgetown University Press, 2018. ISBN 9781626165847 per Open Library listing (the PDF file name carries 9781626165854; title page not checked).
chapter_or_section: Christological Monotheism in the New Testament: 1 Cor 8:6; Phil 2:9-11; John 1:1-18
quote_orig: Worship of Jesus did not infringe Jewish monotheism, because Jesus himself belonged to the unique identity of the one and only God. What is envisaged in this passage of Philippians appears in visionary form in the book of Revelation.
context_before: Bauckham discusses Phil 2:9-11 as an echo of Isa 45:22-23, where YHWH swears that every knee shall bow to him, and says that early Christians "did not see him as an alternative or distinct object of worship alongside God".
what_it_says: Bauckham says Jesus himself belongs to the unique identity of the one God, so worshipping Jesus does not break Jewish monotheism.
claim_supported: (B) early writers (Paul, and the Gospel of John by Bauckham's reading) portray Jesus as sharing YHWH's unique divine identity; (C) early worship of Jesus
scholar_qualification: Bauckham says the NT includes Jesus "in the unique divine identity", not that he is a second god or that he claims YHWH's name. He notes Jesus is "the Son" for whom the term "God" is "only very occasionally used, but 'the Lord' is frequently used" (p. 10), and Paul "never or hardly ever uses the word 'God' of Jesus" (p. 13). His argument is about the NT as a whole, not about Jesus' own words in the Gospels.
limits: Read in the PDF text layer and checked against the rendered page image (dl/page_georgetown_p38.png). The PDF is the full book (216 pages). The printed page is PDF page minus 25 for this chapter (PDF 38 = printed 13). Jesus and the God of Israel (2008) and God Crucified (1998) not read.

edition: Mosher, Lucinda A. and David Marshall, eds. Monotheism and Its Complexities: Christian and Muslim Perspectives. Washington, DC: Georgetown University Press, 2018. ISBN 9781626165847 per Open Library listing (the PDF file name carries 9781626165854; title page not checked).
quote_orig: Paul must mean that Jesus Christ was not some created assistant to God but himself belonged eternally to the unique identity of the one God. By reformulating the Shemaʿ, Paul has expressed this without either denying the distinction between Jesus and God or making Jesus a second god.
context_before: Bauckham argues that 1 Cor 8:6 splits the Shema between God the Father and Jesus Christ, and that Jesus is assigned a role in creation, which Jews reserved for God alone.
what_it_says: Paul includes Jesus in the unique identity of the one God without making Jesus a second god.
claim_supported: (B) earliest Christians (Paul) place Jesus within YHWH's unique identity
scholar_qualification: Bauckham explicitly rejects "ditheism" and does not say Paul calls Jesus God. His claim concerns Paul's theology, not the Gospels.
limits: Read in the PDF text layer; PDF page 37 = printed page 12 (the header "12 Richard Bauckham" is on the page). Page image not separately rendered (the page is in the same PDF).

edition: Mosher, Lucinda A. and David Marshall, eds. Monotheism and Its Complexities: Christian and Muslim Perspectives. Washington, DC: Georgetown University Press, 2018. ISBN 9781626165847 per Open Library listing (the PDF file name carries 9781626165854; title page not checked).
quote_orig: In the self-abasing love of the crucified Jesus, the nations can recognize the deity of the true God. And so, at Jesus’s exaltation to the cosmic throne, God bestows on him his own personal name YHWH, and it is to Jesus that every knee shall bow.
context_before: Bauckham reads Phil 2:9-11 against Isa 45:22-23 and says the passage implies that the incarnation and death of Jesus served the universal worship of the one true God.
what_it_says: Bauckham says that at his exaltation God gives Jesus the personal name YHWH.
claim_supported: (A) as Bauckham reads it, Jesus receives YHWH's personal name (a claim about the divine identity in Philippians, not in the Gospels); (B)
scholar_qualification: This is Bauckham's reading of Phil 2 with Isa 45, not a claim that Jesus called himself YHWH in the Gospels. The Philippians text itself does not name YHWH; the name is inferred from the Isaiah echo.
limits: Read in the PDF text layer and in the page image (PDF p. 38).

edition: Mosher, Lucinda A. and David Marshall, eds. Monotheism and Its Complexities: Christian and Muslim Perspectives. Washington, DC: Georgetown University Press, 2018. ISBN 9781626165847 per Open Library listing (the PDF file name carries 9781626165854; title page not checked).
quote_orig: He wishes to provide his readers from the start with the insight into Jesus’s identity that the characters in his story attain only at the end of the story (cf. John 20:28): that Jesus is God incarnate.
context_before: Bauckham discusses the prologue of John's Gospel, which begins with "In the beginning" as Genesis does, and says the Word "was God" while also "with God".
what_it_says: Bauckham reads John's prologue as presenting from the start the identity that the characters discover only at the end (Thomas, John 20:28): that Jesus is God incarnate.

quote_orig: But, to underscore a point registered already, the most striking innovation in early Jesus-devotion was the programmatic incorporation of Jesus as recipient of formal, cultic devotion.
context_before: Hurtado argues that Jewish principal-agent traditions (including principal angels) are background for early Christology, but that the devotion to Jesus went beyond them.

scholar: Bart D. Ehrman (on Gospel of John claims)
work: How Jesus Became God (HarperOne, 2014), as discussed in the NPR Fresh Air interview of 7 April 2014
edition: NPR web page (book page not read)
chapter_or_section: Interview: Gospel of John vs. Synoptics
quote_orig: You do find Jesus calling himself God in the Gospel of John, or the last Gospel. Jesus says things like, "Before Abraham was, I am." And, "I and the Father are one," and, "If you've seen me, you've seen the Father." These are all statements you find only in the Gospel of John, and that's striking because we have earlier gospels and we have the writings of Paul, and in none of them is there any indication that Jesus said such things.
context_before: Asked about the difference between the Synoptics and John, Ehrman says the divine claims are in John.
what_it_says: Ehrman says the Gospel of John has Jesus calling himself God and cites John 8:58 and 10:30 as examples; he says these claims appear only in John.
claim_supported: (A) the John sayings that Ehrman treats as the explicit claims (John 8:58, 10:30; 14:9) and his argument that they are not historical
scholar_qualification: Ehrman's argument is that these sayings appear only in John and reflect the Gospel's theology, not that Jesus did not speak in the Gospel's terms. He writes: "I think it's completely implausible that Matthew, Mark and Luke would not mention that Jesus called himself God if that's what he was declaring about himself." That is an argument from silence and is contested.
